readingInstruction: Read Proverbs 9:1-11:31. Chapter 9 closes the first major section with two rival invitations. Chapters 10 and 11 begin the collection of short sayings. Notice the change of style.
settingTheScene: Chapter 9 ends the long introduction with a banquet scene. Lady Wisdom and the woman Folly both call out from the heights of the city, but one leads to life and the other to the grave. Then, beginning at chapter 10, the book changes. The long speeches give way to short two-line sayings, mostly about the contrast between the righteous and the wicked. These are the proverbs most people think of.
observation: “Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars” (9:1).
“Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight” (9:6).
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight” (9:10).
“The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing” (9:13).
“But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol” (9:18).
“A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish son is a sorrow to his mother” (10:1).
“When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom” (11:2).
“Whoever brings blessing will be enriched, and one who waters will himself be watered” (11:25).
interpretation:
The picture in chapter 9 is of two banquets. Wisdom has built her house, prepared her meat, mixed her wine, and sent out her servants. The invitation is open to the simple. Folly also sits at the door of her house, on the high places of the city, calling to those passing by. The words are similar, but the end is different. “He does not know that the dead are there.” The meal that looks like life is the doorway to death.

The chapter’s lesson is that no one is neutral. Everyone is eating at one of the two tables. We are being formed either by wisdom or by folly. And verse 10 repeats the theme: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.”

Chapter 10 begins the first collection of sayings attributed to Solomon. They are scattered, not organized by topic, and the reader is meant to take them one at a time, like a string of pearls. Many are contrasts: the righteous and the wicked, the diligent and the lazy, the wise and the fool.

It is important to read proverbs as proverbs. They are general truths about how the world tends to work, not promises that apply in every case. “The hand of the diligent will rule” is generally true. It is not a guarantee. Proverbs describe the grain of the world, the way things usually go when God’s moral order is at work. The book of Job and Ecclesiastes will later explore the exceptions.

Several themes emerge in these chapters: honest speech, generosity, humility, and the danger of pride. “Whoever is generous will be blessed.” “One gives freely, yet grows all the richer.” Generosity is not a loss but a form of wisdom. The righteous are described as a tree of life, a “fruit” that helps others. And “whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf.”
connection: Jesus told parables of two houses (Matthew 7:24-27) and two banquets (Luke 14:15-24), and spoke of the narrow and wide gates (Matthew 7:13-14). He is the true wisdom who sends out his servants with the invitation to come to the feast (Matthew 22:1-10). He said, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35), echoing 11:25. Proverbs 11:30 (“the fruit of the righteous is a tree of life”) points to Revelation 22:2.
application:
Ask which table you are eating at today. What is feeding you: wisdom or folly?

Practice one act of generosity this week and watch what it does to your heart.

Read proverbs one at a time, and slowly. Choose one to think about throughout the day.
prayerPrompts: Accept Wisdom’s invitation, and tell God what that means for you.
Ask him to keep you from the table of Folly.
Thank Christ for spreading a feast for you.
